uv: the cleanest way to manage Python

The problem it solves

Python environments are the classic mess. There is the system Python and the project Python, pip next to conda next to poetry next to pipx, a virtual environment you have to remember to activate, a requirements.txt that nobody pinned and a version that works on one machine only. Coding agents make it worse: left alone they happily pip install into whatever Python they find first.

The general idea

uv is one fast tool, written in Rust, for all of it: Python versions, virtual environments, dependencies, a lockfile, scripts and command-line tools. A project is a pyproject.toml, a uv.lock and a .venv that uv manages for you. You never activate anything: uv run always runs inside the right, up-to-date environment, creating or syncing it first if needed. That makes it the cleanest way I know to manage Python, for me and for the agents.

Examples

A new project, dependencies and a test run:

uv init analysis && cd analysis
uv add duckdb pydantic
uv add --dev pytest ruff pyright
uv run pytest

Pin the Python version of the project, and run a tool without installing it:

uv python pin 3.13
uvx ruff check

A single script can carry its own dependencies in a comment, and uv run builds a throwaway environment for it:

# /// script
# dependencies = ["requests"]
# ///
import requests
print(requests.get("https://example.com").status_code)
uv run script.py

Tips from my setup

  • One line in CLAUDE.md tells every agent that I use uv and that packages are added with uv add. Since then nothing gets installed into a random Python. See the post about my Claude setup.
  • uv run everywhere. My tv channel runs tests with uv run pytest, the Neovim REPL starts uv run python, and my just recipes call uv run, so tools and editor always use the project environment.
  • A dependency for one run only. A helper recipe that reads a YAML file is started with uv run --with pyyaml python3 script.py: pyyaml is available for that run and installed nowhere.
  • Commit the lockfile. The laptop, the computer at home and the agent all get exactly the same packages, which matters when a job runs on one machine and I check it from another.
  • Environments are cheap. Because creating one is so fast, a throwaway environment for an experiment is no longer a decision.
  • Few, plain packages. uv makes adding a dependency easy, so I keep the habit of writing vanilla Python with dataclasses, pydantic and numpy and limiting what gets imported.
